# CVE-2026-129360 — Magma orc8r Obsidian REST: the operator identity follows the spoofable `X-Magma-Client-Cert-Serial` header

[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg)](LICENSE)
[![Research status: validated](https://img.shields.io/badge/research-validated%20differential-success.svg)](#5-expected-results)

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **CVE** | CVE-2026-129360 |
| **Component** | Linux Foundation Magma orc8r — `orc8r/cloud/go/services/obsidian/access/operator.go` (`getOperator`) behind `CertificateMiddleware` (`rest_middleware.go`) |
| **Affected** | Magma ≤ 1.9.0 (logic unchanged in master at lab time) |
| **Fixed in** | nothing upstream at the time of this laboratory; the fixed side is a hash-checked synthetic remediation (documented as such) |
| **CWE** | CWE-290 (Authentication Bypass by Spoofing) |
| **Impact** | Operator impersonation on the NMS/obsidian REST tier: a caller who knows (or guesses) a registered operator certificate serial authenticates as that operator with nothing but a header — certificate serials are not secret, and no certificate possession is checked |
| **Vector** | Network — an HTTP request carrying `X-Magma-Client-Cert-Serial: <registered operator serial>` |
| **Trigger** | the header value alone; unknown serials are rejected through the real certifier lookup |

The obsidian REST tier resolves the caller's identity from a header:

```go
// orc8r/cloud/go/services/obsidian/access/operator.go
csn := req.Header.Get(CLIENT_CERT_SN_KEY)            // attacker-controlled header
certInfo, err := certifier.GetCertificateIdentity(req.Context(), csn)
...
return certInfo.Id, nil                               // operator identity
```

The design assumes a trusted TLS-terminating proxy injects that header
from the **verified** client certificate. When the header is reachable
by the client (direct service exposure, a proxy that forwards
client-supplied headers, or any topology where the assumption breaks),
knowing a registered operator **serial** — which is not a secret — is
the whole authentication. This laboratory runs the **real**
`CertificateMiddleware` behind the **real** certifier client against a
certifier gRPC server implementing the **real** protobuf service with
one registered operator certificate, and proves the spoof: t

# CVE-2026-129359 — Magma orc8r: the hardcoded inter-service credential `7ZZXAF7CAETF241KL22B8YRR7B5UF401` authenticates any gRPC caller as a trusted internal cloud service

[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg)](LICENSE)

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **CVE** | CVE-2026-129359 |
| **Component** | Linux Foundation Magma orc8r — `orc8r/lib/go/registry/interceptors.go` (the constant) and `orc8r/cloud/go/service/middleware/unary/identity_decorator.go` (the accepting check) |
| **Affected** | Magma ≤ 1.9.0 (the constant and the accepting branch are unchanged in master) |
| **Fixed in** | nothing upstream at the time of this laboratory; the fixed side here is a hash-checked one-line synthetic remediation (documented as such) |
| **CWE** | CWE-798 (Use of Hard-coded Credentials) |
| **Impact** | Authentication bypass at the orc8r gRPC tier: any network client that can reach an orchestrator service port and knows the public constant is treated as a trusted internal cloud call — the same trust level as an in-cluster service, with no certificate, no identity, and no lookup |
| **Vector** | Network — a gRPC call carrying `x-magma-client-cert-serial: 7ZZXAF7CAETF241KL22B8YRR7B5UF401` |
| **Trigger** | the exact constant; every other serial goes through the real certifier lookup and is rejected when unknown |

Magma's cloud services authenticate each other with a shared secret that
was never secret: the constant
`ORC8R_CLIENT_CERT_VALUE = "7ZZXAF7CAETF241KL22B8YRR7B5UF401"` ships in
the public source, is attached by internal clients to every inter-service
call, and — on the server side — is accepted verbatim with zero
verification:

```go
// orc8r/lib/go/registry/interceptors.go
ORC8R_CLIENT_CERT_VALUE = "7ZZXAF7CAETF241KL22B8YRR7B5UF401"   // public since 2020

// orc8r/cloud/go/service/middleware/unary/identity_decorator.go
func findIdentityFromUniqueCSN(ctx context.Context, sn string, ...) {
    if sn == registry.ORC8R_CLIENT_CERT_VALUE {
        return newCtx, nil        // trusted internal cloud call — no lookup
    }
    ...                          // every other serial: real certifier lookup
```

# Changelog

All notable changes to this project are listed here. Versions follow semantic versioning.

## Unreleased

### Security

- **fleet checks the host ssh will actually reach, through your ssh config, and its jump hosts, and pins it.**

  What was wrong: the gate checked the destination as written (or the system resolver's answer for it), while ssh applied `HostName`, `Match`, `ProxyJump` and `ProxyCommand` from the operator's ssh config, which the gate never read. With `--scope 10.0.0.0/24`, `db-01` (resolver: 10.0.0.7, config: `HostName 198.51.100.9`) and `10.0.0.5` (config: `ProxyJump jump.example.test`) were both listed as in scope and both sessions were started, to hosts outside the scope. A host covered through a network entry was also resolved again by ssh, so the session was not tied to the checked address. Jump hosts were never checked at all, and ssh's own `ProxyJump` passes only `-l`, `-p`, `-J`, `-F` and `-v` to a hop, so every hop ran without `BatchMode` and the other options the tool gives the session.

  What changed: before the gate, `modes.vet_fleet_target` runs the configured ssh binary with `-G` (no connection; 10 second timeout, 64 KiB of output) and the session's own options and command, and checks the `hostname` it reports. That hostname must be a plain address or a plain name (see the entry on trailing dots). A hostname covered by name is left to ssh. One covered only through a network entry is resolved once and the session is pinned with `-o HostName=<address> -o HostKeyAlias=<hostname> -o StrictHostKeyChecking=yes` (the alias is port-qualified for a port other than 22, or is the configured alias), so host key checking looks for the name and a key not already known fails instead of being trusted on first use. `ssh -G` is run again with the pin and that answer is checked, because a `Match host` block keyed on the address can add a `ProxyJump` only then.
